children: Kevin Warsh’s first Jackson Hole speech as Federal Reserve chair has put a familiar question back on the table for global investors: how much should they pay for growth when the world’s most important central bank is signalling that inflation still matters more than markets may want?

For India, the answer could determine whether foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) continue buying domestic equities or return to looking for better-valued opportunities elsewhere. FPIs have been net buyers for two straight months, buying nearly $5 billion in Indian equities in July and August — the first such streak since November. Whether that buying continues could depend increasingly on relative valuations and India’s premium over emerging markets.

As of August 31, MSCI India’s forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio stood at 19.65 times, compared with 9.93 times for emerging markets. The valuation gap has actually widened marginally over the past month: on July 31, MSCI India traded at 20.32 times forward earnings against 10.35 times for MSCI EM, implying a premium of about 96%. By August 31, the premium had risen to about 98%, even as valuations in both markets moderated.

Warsh said US inflation remains well above the Fed’s 2% target and made it clear that the central bank would not commit itself to a fixed path for interest rates. He also said broad financial conditions in the US were not restrictive, with credit markets still showing considerable strength.
That raises the prospect of a higher cost of capital for longer. And when the cost of capital rises, markets generally have to reassess how much they are willing to pay for future earnings.
Ed Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research, believes the Fed may need to go further than talking tough.
“I think it does need to do, which is gain some credibility by actually raising the Fed funds rate by 25 basis points in September. I think it’s going to happen,” Yardeni said.
A global valuation reset could put frothy markets first
The first pressure from a higher-for-longer Fed is unlikely to fall equally across markets.

Stocks and markets where valuations have run far ahead of current earnings are more exposed because higher interest rates reduce the value investors place on profits expected many years into the future.

The so-called Magnificent Seven in the US (US technology giants, comprising Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Nvidia and Tesla) and parts of Asia, particularly South Korea, that have rallied strongly on the artificial intelligence theme could therefore face a sharper valuation reset.
For emerging markets, the question then becomes one of relative value.
Is India still too expensive for foreign investors?

MSCI India has usually traded at a premium to the broader emerging markets index. While both Indian and emerging-market valuations have moderated, India’s premium has remained elevated and edged higher over the past month, even as foreign investors returned to buying.
The real question is not whether Indian stocks are expensive, but whether they are too expensive compared with other emerging markets.

If the valuation gap remains large, higher US interest rates could push global investors towards cheaper markets offering similar growth prospects. But if India's earnings growth can justify the premium, the current global reset could eventually help attract foreign money back.

That is important because the latest FPI buying marks a tentative shift in flows, rather than necessarily a broad-based return of foreign capital. FPIs sold more than $27 billion worth of Indian equities between March and June before buying $2.45 billion in July and another $2.12 billion in August.
Much of the recent buying has also been selective, with block deals, QIPs and offers for sale accounting for a significant portion of the inflows.

Improving earnings visibility has provided some support. The combined net profit of Nifty 500 companies rose 13% year-on-year to ₹4.4 lakh crore in the June quarter, while revenue increased 21% to ₹39.2 lakh crore, according to Bloomberg data.

Kotak Institutional Equities also sees earnings growth broadening. It said Nifty 500 companies recorded 20% year-on-year revenue growth and 10% profit growth in the first quarter of FY27, while consensus estimates point to 13% and 18% earnings growth in FY27 and FY28, respectively.

Motilal Oswal, however, has highlighted valuations as one of the factors that had kept foreign sentiment weak. Its July strategy report said “geopolitical uncertainties, moderating earnings growth, and elevated valuations” had contributed to cumulative FII outflows of $58 billion over the 22 months since the Indian market peaked in September 2024.
The report also showed how domestic investors have increasingly cushioned foreign selling. DII ownership of the Nifty 500 rose to a record 21% in June 2026, while FII ownership fell to 17%.
Yardeni's comments also highlight the importance of bond markets. He said a 25-basis-point Fed rate hike could even lower bond yields if investors see it as a strong move against inflation.

For India, the reaction of US Treasury yields, the dollar and India's 10-year bond yield may matter more than the Fed decision itself. Higher US yields and a stronger dollar could keep pressure on the rupee and make Indian assets less attractive. Stable bond markets, however, could limit the impact on emerging markets.

Within equities, the effect may vary. Expensive growth stocks could face the biggest pressure, while financials, healthcare and industrial companies with more reasonable valuations may hold up better.

The key question for Indian markets this week is not just whether the Nifty falls after Jackson Hole. It is whether investors reassess how much they are willing to pay for India's growth story — and whether that makes Indian stocks attractive enough for foreign investors to continue buying.
That could make MSCI India's valuation premium over emerging markets the most important number to watch.

title: Kevin Warsh's Fed message puts India’s valuation premium to test
